dbdbe70d91.q: How should hospitality brands build customer connection when the founder or staff are not physically present in the store?
dbdbe70d91.a: Danny Meyer recommends thinking of the product packaging itself as your brand ambassador or bartender. He suggests using the can or package as a tool to be playful and create unexpected moments, referencing how Liquid Death uses messaging like 'murder your thirst' on their cans. He points to Ramona canned wine, created by sommelier Jordan Salcedo, as an example where customers feel personally connected to the founder when purchasing the product.
dbdbe70d91.e: Advice Line with Danny Meyer of Shake Shack

14b407be74.q: How does Danny Meyer define and measure company culture in hospitality and restaurants?
14b407be74.a: Meyer defines culture as 'how we do things around here' and has evolved from using family values to what he calls 'expected behaviors.' He created an equation: culture equals all wanted behaviors that you actively celebrate minus all unwanted behaviors that you tolerate. This shift was necessary because calling a business a family became disingenuous when needing to hold people accountable and potentially let them go.
14b407be74.e: Advice Line with Danny Meyer of Shake Shack

a16968d212.q: Should a startup with early retail success in Whole Foods expand direct-to-consumer shipping before consolidating store distribution?
a16968d212.a: Guy Raz advises waiting and starting small with limited geographic experiments before major DTC expansion, emphasizing the importance of tracking repeat orders as the key success metric. Danny Meyer agrees but adds a contrarian point: it's worth testing limited DTC on platforms like Goldbelly one or two days per week to gather national demand data without adding capacity, even if you're not ready for full expansion.
a16968d212.e: Advice Line with Danny Meyer of Shake Shack

85922c0b75.q: What is the 'day one mentality' philosophy that has kept Danny Meyer's restaurants relevant for decades?
85922c0b75.a: Meyer explains that the day one mentality asks teams to imagine it's their opening day, remembering the pride of pristine conditions and perfect plates. He notes that Union Square Cafe is 41 years old, Gramercy Tavern is 31, Shake Shack is 22, and The Modern is 22 because 'every day we ask our teams to imagine that it's day one,' assuming three restaurant critics are in the audience on any given night.
85922c0b75.e: Advice Line with Danny Meyer of Shake Shack

f50f11eea5.q: How can you tell if a restaurant genuinely has a culture of hospitality or is just talking about it?
f50f11eea5.a: Meyer says to look at the staff members when you walk in: if they are focused on doing their job well and having fun with each other, checking both boxes, that joy de vivre becomes an ingredient in your meal. He notes that many restaurants achieve technical perfection but lack love, and he avoids returning to those places. The same applies to airlines—watch flight attendants to see if they're focused and playful with each other.

88cab4df98.q: How did growing up on a farm influence early interest in cosmetic formulation and chemistry?
88cab4df98.a: Karissa started formulating makeup in her parents' kitchen at age 10, learning chemistry through imagination and experimentation. She ground down sunflower seeds to make butter, steamed rose petals for pigment, and discovered that blackberries could stain hands, realizing this pigment could be used in lipstick or blush. Her parents fostered this creativity by providing her with books like the Cosmetic Ingredient Dictionary before the internet era.

c5bc538a72.q: What opportunities did working at Sephora provide compared to other retail beauty positions?
c5bc538a72.a: At Sephora, Karissa was trained on every single brand and received multiple certifications in artistry, skincare, fragrance, and hair care through different levels. She credited Sephora with raising her and providing her real education in beauty, whereas she had applied to all the beauty counters at other retailers and was rejected because she didn't have the skill set they were looking for at the time.

bd72e7e3b1.q: What role did Clarisonic and L'Oreal play in shaping a career in product development?
bd72e7e3b1.a: Clarisonic was a sonic cleansing brush created by the same five founders who pioneered Sonicare, based in Factoria, Washington. While Karissa was working at Sephora, Clarisonic was acquired by L'Oreal within her first year there. Carol Hamilton, president of L'Oreal Lux, saw potential in Karissa and took her to Paris to work with chemists and engineers on luxury brand collaborations, creating devices for Yves Saint Laurent and Lancôme.

4dfcec4c41.q: How did a friend's death from cancer inspire a shift toward purpose-driven entrepreneurship?
4dfcec4c41.a: In 2013, Christy Lamond, a college friend who dedicated her life to philanthropy and taught English to young girls in Tanzania and Chile, died of cancer at age 24. While Karissa was in Paris presenting to the CEO of L'Oreal at their annual Mondial conference, Christy called to say she had cancer, and she passed away nine months later. Christy's blog 'Wake Up and Live' discussed dying successfully, which profoundly influenced Karissa's decision to leave L'Oreal and create a brand with purpose.
4dfcec4c41.e: Thrive Causemetics: Karissa Bodnar. How a Beauty Business Made Millions for a Mission

99a32c030b.q: What specific problem in the beauty industry for cancer patients inspired the creation of Thrive Causemetics?
99a32c030b.a: While volunteering as a makeup artist with Look Good, Feel Better, an organization providing makeup classes to women going through cancer, Karissa discovered that women who had lost their natural lashes had no solution. Traditional mascara wouldn't work without lashes, and fake lashes with toxic glues filled with latex, parabens, and sulfates were irritating to immune-compromised people and wouldn't stay on. She wanted to create a non-toxic solution that would help people like Christy maintain their dignity and sense of self.
99a32c030b.e: Thrive Causemetics: Karissa Bodnar. How a Beauty Business Made Millions for a Mission

b69ed39341.q: How did the Tom's Shoes business model influence the founding approach of Thrive Cosmetics?
b69ed39341.a: Karissa woke up in the middle of the night in Los Angeles during an L'Oreal trip in 2013 and thought about how Tom's had built an engine for giving back through its shoe company. She realized the beauty industry had the budget to give back in a more meaningful way, and she decided to apply that one-for-one model to create Thrive Causemetics as a purpose-driven beauty brand.

c92c5017a4.q: What financial commitment and employment strategy did Karissa use to launch Thrive Causemetics?
c92c5017a4.a: Karissa invested approximately $100,000 of her life savings into starting Thrive Cosmetics. She also worked a full-time job in a different category—the nutrition and coffee industry at Bulletproof Coffee Company—to ensure she remained gainfully employed, as her father had always stressed the importance of maintaining employment while building the business.

Sales were mainly online and tiny—a good day was $100 in revenue, and there were many days with no sales. She wiped out her entire life savings funding production through her full-time job.
